title: React State Management: useState to Stores
summary: A study-notes handbook on how React state actually works — from useState and the render/commit cycle, through useReducer, Context, and re-render cost, to the rules for when a local hook is enough and when you need an external store.

chapters.title: What State Is in React
points: Definition: state = any value that changes over time and must trigger a re-render when it changes
Props vs state: props flow down and are read-only to the child; state is owned and mutated by the component that declares it
State vs plain variable: `let count = 0` inside a component resets every render and never triggers re-render
State vs ref: `useRef().current` survives renders but changing it does NOT re-render — use for timer ids, DOM nodes, previous values
Derived state is not state: `const fullName = first + ' ' + last` should be computed during render, never stored in a second useState
Four categories of app data: local UI state, form state, URL state, server cache state — each wants a different tool
Server cache is not client state: data fetched from an API is a cache with staleness, not something a reducer should own
React is a pure function of state: `UI = f(state)` — the same state must produce the same tree
Single source of truth: any value duplicated in two places will drift
Example: `isOpen` belongs in state; `openedAtTimestamp` used only for logging belongs in a ref

chapters.title: useState: The Basic Hook
points: Signature: `const [value, setValue] = useState(initialValue)` returns a tuple, destructured by position
Initial value is used only on the first render of that component instance; later renders ignore the argument
Lazy initializer: pass a function `useState(() => expensiveParse(json))` so the work runs once, not every render
`useState(expensiveParse(json))` still calls expensiveParse on every render — the result is just discarded
Functional updater: `setCount(c => c + 1)` reads the latest queued value; `setCount(count + 1)` reads the render's closure snapshot
Example: three `setCount(count + 1)` calls in a row increment by 1; three `setCount(c => c + 1)` increment by 3
State is immutable by contract: `items.push(x); setItems(items)` does nothing because the reference is unchanged
Immutable update patterns: `[...items, x]`, `items.filter(i => i.id !== id)`, `{...obj, key: v}`
Bailout: if the new value is `Object.is`-equal to the current one, React may skip the re-render
Setter identity is stable across renders — safe to omit from dependency arrays
Resetting state on prop change: prefer a `key` prop on the child over a useEffect that calls the setter

chapters.title: How a State Update Actually Runs
points: Render is a phase, not a paint: React calls the component function to produce a description of UI
Three phases: render (compute), reconcile (diff against previous tree), commit (apply DOM mutations)
Update queue: each setState call pushes an update onto that hook's queue; the queue is drained at the start of the next render
Batching: multiple setState calls in one event handler produce one re-render
React 18+ automatic batching extends this to promises, setTimeout, and native event handlers — React 17 batched only React events
`flushSync(() => setX(v))` opts out of batching when you must read layout immediately after
State is a closure snapshot: the `count` inside a handler is the value from the render that created that handler
Example: `setCount(count+1); console.log(count)` logs the OLD value — the variable is const in this render
Hooks are stored as a linked list on the fiber, matched by call order — hence the rules of hooks
Rules of hooks: no hooks in conditions, loops, or after early returns; only in components and custom hooks
Re-render of a parent re-renders all children by default, regardless of whether their props changed

chapters.title: useReducer: State as Transitions
points: Signature: `const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init?)`
Reducer shape: `(state, action) => newState` — a pure function, no fetches, no mutations, no Math.random
Action shape convention: `{ type: 'added', payload }`; a switch over `action.type` with a `default: throw`
Third argument `init` is a lazy initializer: `useReducer(reducer, userId, createInitialState)`
`dispatch` has a stable identity forever — safe in deps, safe to pass deep through context without memoization
Example: a cart reducer handling `add`, `remove`, `setQty`, `clear` in one place instead of four setters
Use when the next state depends on the previous one in non-trivial ways, or when several fields must change together
Use when the same update logic fires from many places — the reducer is the single edit surface
Impossible states: model `{status: 'idle'|'loading'|'error'|'success'}` instead of three independent booleans
Reducers are trivially unit-testable: call with a state and an action, assert the output — no React needed
Mistake: mutating `state.items.push()` inside the reducer instead of returning a new object
Mistake: dispatching in a loop expecting to read the result — dispatch is async relative to the current render

chapters.title: useState vs useReducer
points: Row — number of fields: useState for 1-2 independent values; useReducer once fields are coupled
Row — update logic location: useState scatters it into handlers; useReducer centralizes it into one pure function
Row — testability: useState logic tests need a component; a reducer tests as a plain function
Row — debugging: reducers give you a named action per change, ideal for logging every transition
Row — code volume: useReducer costs boilerplate that is pure overhead for a single toggle
Row — identity stability: setter and dispatch are both stable; no advantage either way
They are the same primitive underneath — useState is implemented as a useReducer with a basic reducer
Migration path: start with useState, switch when you find yourself calling three setters in one handler
Anti-pattern: one `useReducer` holding unrelated slices just to avoid multiple useState calls
Anti-pattern: `useState({a, b, c})` then spreading on every update — you built a worse reducer
Example side-by-side: a form with validation as five useState calls vs one reducer with `field_changed`/`submitted`

chapters.title: Lifting State and Prop Drilling
points: Lifting up: when two siblings need the same value, move it to their closest common ancestor and pass it down
Controlled vs uncontrolled: a controlled input takes `value` + `onChange` from the parent; an uncontrolled one keeps its own DOM state
Colocation rule: push state as far DOWN as it can go — the smallest subtree that needs it re-renders
Prop drilling: threading a value through components that do not use it, only to reach a deep consumer
Drilling is a readability problem first and a refactor-friction problem second — it is not a performance bug
Composition as the cure: pass JSX as `children` or as a prop so the deep node is created by the owner of the state
Example: `<Layout sidebar={<UserMenu user={user} />} />` skips passing `user` through Layout entirely
Three or four levels of drilling is usually fine; reaching for context at level two is premature
Mistake: copying a prop into state (`useState(props.value)`) — the copy goes stale when the prop changes
Summary rule: lift only as high as the nearest shared owner, never to the root by reflex

chapters.title: Context: Broadcast, Not Store
points: Three pieces: `createContext(default)`, `<Ctx.Provider value={...}>`, `useContext(Ctx)` in the consumer
Context solves distribution, not storage — the state still lives in a useState or useReducer above the provider
Default value applies only when no matching Provider exists above; a common source of silent bugs
Propagation: any consumer re-renders when the provider's `value` changes by `Object.is`, no matter how deep
Context re-renders bypass `React.memo` on components between provider and consumer
The classic bug: `value={{user, setUser}}` creates a new object every render, so every consumer re-renders always
Fix: `const value = useMemo(() => ({user, setUser}), [user])`
Splitting contexts: a `StateContext` and a separate `DispatchContext` so action-only components never re-render on data changes
The reducer + two contexts pattern: dispatch is stable, so the dispatch context value never changes
Nested providers override outward-in; useContext reads the nearest one
Best fits: theme, locale, auth session, feature flags — low-frequency, app-wide values
Poor fits: values that change per keystroke or per animation frame with many consumers

chapters.title: Re-render Cost and Memoization
points: A re-render is not a repaint: React still diffs and commits nothing if the output is unchanged — the cost is the JS work
Default rule: when a component re-renders, its entire subtree re-renders
`React.memo(Component)` skips a re-render when props are shallow-equal to the previous props
memo is defeated by any inline object, array, or arrow function prop — a new reference every render
`useMemo(() => value, deps)` caches a value; `useCallback(fn, deps)` caches a function reference
useCallback(fn, deps) is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps)
Memoization is not free: it costs allocation plus a dependency comparison on every render
Wrong fix order: measure with the React DevTools Profiler before adding memo — most re-renders are cheap
Structural fix beats memo: move state down, or wrap the expensive subtree in `children` so it is not re-created
Context selector problem: useContext cannot subscribe to part of a value — external stores can
`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot)` is the official hook for subscribing to state outside React
Mistake: memoizing everything by default, producing code that is slower and much harder to read

chapters.title: When to Reach for a Store
points: Signal 1: the same state is read by distant, unrelated subtrees and lifting it means hoisting to the root
Signal 2: high-frequency updates with many consumers, where context would re-render the whole tree
Signal 3: you need selector subscriptions — a component that re-renders only when `state.cart.total` changes
Signal 4: state must live outside the React tree — read or written from a websocket handler, an interceptor, a service worker
Signal 5: you need time-travel, persistence, or a serialized action log for debugging
External store mechanics: a module-level object plus a subscriber set; components subscribe via useSyncExternalStore
Redux Toolkit: single store, slices, Immer-backed mutation syntax, DevTools and middleware — heaviest, most structured
Zustand: hook-based store with `useStore(s => s.slice)` selectors, no provider required, minimal boilerplate
Jotai / Recoil: atomic model — many small atoms, derived atoms recompute automatically, bottom-up
MobX: observable objects with automatic dependency tracking; re-renders come from proxy reads, not from setState
TanStack Query / SWR: not a client store — a server-cache layer with staleness, dedupe, refetch, and retry
The real lesson: most 'we need Redux' cases are actually server cache plus a couple of contexts
Cost of a store: an extra mental model, indirection on every read, and lint rules the team must actually follow

chapters.title: Async, Effects and Server State
points: Effects are for synchronizing with external systems, not for computing values from other state
The fetch-in-useEffect pattern and its four bugs: race conditions, no cleanup, double-invoke in StrictMode, no cache
Race fix: an `ignore` flag or an AbortController in the cleanup function
StrictMode in development mounts, unmounts, and remounts once — effects run twice on purpose to surface missing cleanup
Loading state as a union: `{status, data, error}` in one reducer beats `isLoading` + `data` + `error` as three useState calls
Do not mirror props or server data into state; render from the source or from a query cache
`useEffect` with an object dependency re-runs every render because the reference is new each time
`useTransition` marks an update non-urgent so typing stays responsive while a heavy list re-renders
`useDeferredValue(value)` renders a stale value while the expensive update happens in the background
`useOptimistic` shows a predicted result immediately and reverts if the action fails
Server Components move data fetching out of the client entirely — no client state involved for read-only data
Mistake: a useEffect that calls setState with a value derivable during render, causing a guaranteed double render

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Anti-Patterns
points: Storing derived data in state, then adding an effect to keep it in sync — compute it during render instead
Copying props into state and expecting updates to flow through; use `key` to reset, or read the prop directly
Mutating state objects or arrays in place, then wondering why nothing re-rendered
Reading state right after setting it and logging the stale closure value
Using a state variable where a ref belongs, causing a re-render on every mouse move or timer tick
Passing a fresh object as a context value with no useMemo — every consumer re-renders on every parent render
Putting everything in one global context so the whole app re-renders when a single flag flips
Wrapping every callback in useCallback while the children are not memoized — pure overhead
Redundant state: `items` plus `itemCount` plus `hasItems`, three values that must be kept in agreement
Booleans that encode a state machine badly: `isLoading && isError` is a reachable, meaningless combination
Using an effect to respond to a user event when the logic belongs directly in the event handler
Reaching for Redux to hold API responses that a query library would cache, dedupe, and refetch for free

chapters.title: Decision Guide and Cheatsheet
points: Decision ladder: plain variable → ref → useState → useReducer → lift up → context → external store
One component owns it, few fields → useState
One component, coupled fields or many transitions → useReducer
Two siblings need it → lift to nearest common parent
Deep subtree needs it, changes rarely → context (memoized value, split state and dispatch)
Whole app, changes often, needs selectors → external store (Zustand / Redux Toolkit / Jotai)
It came from a server → query cache (TanStack Query / SWR), not client state
It should survive reload or be shareable → URL params, then localStorage
API recall: `useState(init)`, `useState(() => init)`, `setX(v)`, `setX(prev => next)`
API recall: `useReducer(reducer, initArg, init)`, `dispatch({type, payload})`
API recall: `createContext`, `<Ctx.Provider value>`, `useContext`, `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot)`
Perf recall: `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, `flushSync`
Rules to keep: state immutable, hooks unconditional, state colocated, derived values computed not stored
Final principle: reach for the smallest tool that removes the pain you actually measured
